title: Hosted API Demo - Chat & Text Generation Basics
summary: Intro/demo of Redwood hosted API focused on chat/text generation: streaming responses, key params (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), retry semantics and idempotency, simple retry/backoff patterns, and next steps to run a short benchmark. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated for latency-sensitive scoring pipelines; security/audit logs and SSO are must-haves.

Samir Patel: send benchmark guide + sample scripts
Ruth/Derek: schedule dedicated latency test next week

transcript:
Header: Recorded 2026-03-04 14:27 -07:00 | Duration 42m | Redwood: Morgan Lee, Samir Patel, Iris Chen | Highland Finance: Ruth Campbell, Derek Huang, Lena Ortiz, Mark Avery

[00:00] Morgan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joinin today, really quick intro - I'm Morgan from Redwood Inference, and with me are Samir (SE) and Iris from solutions. How's every one doin?
[00:10] Ruth Campbell: Good thanks, Ruth here. Really excited to see the hosted API flow, our team is looking at outcomes for chat-based scoring and some generation tasks.
[00:18] Morgan Lee: Awesome. Quick agenda - walk through hosted API capabilities for chat & text generation, streaming, tuning params, retries and idempotency, then Q&A and next steps.
[00:29] Samir Patel: I'll kick off with a demo of a streaming response - just to set expectations, we stream token-by-token and you can attach a client-side handler. Also note we do prefix/K V cache optimizations, sometimes transcribed as KV cache or K V cache in notes.
[00:45] [00:45] (demo) Samir Patel: Here is a simple chat call, you send messages array, model id, and you get back either a full response or a stream where we send delta tokens. So for latency-sensitive scoring you can start processing partial output.
[01:02] Derek Huang: Sorry can you repeat the part about partial output? We need deterministic latency for scoring pipelines.
[01:07] Samir Patel: Yeah so with streaming you can receive the first tokens in ~30-50ms after model decode begins depending on sequence length; you don't have to wait for full completion. There's tradeoffs though - batching is more efficient for cost but increases tail latency.
[01:22] Ruth Campbell: Sounds good. On params, what's the typical knobs we should tune?
[01:27] Iris Chen: The core ones are temperature, top_p, max_tokens, presence/prompt penalty. Temperature controls randomness; top_p is nucleus sampling. For deterministic scoring we often suggest low temperature (0 - 0.2) and fixed max_tokens.
[01:43] Morgan Lee: We also expose stop sequences and logprobs if you need scoring-based decisions.
[01:48] [02:00] Samir Patel: Quick note about retries - our hosted API returns an idempotency key when you supply one, and also supports retry-after headers on rate limits. For transient 5xx errors we recommend an exponential backoff with jitter. The SDKs include built-in retry logic but you can override.
[02:20] Lena Ortiz: Do you have an example for idempotency? How do we avoid double-cost on retry?
[02:25] Samir Patel: You pass an idempotency_token with your request. If the request actually completed server-side but the client timed out, Redwood will surface the original response. There are edge cases for streaming where partial receipts may need client reconciliation - we can share sample patterns.
[02:40] Mark Avery: What's your SLA on 99p latency or do you have benchmarks?
[02:44] Morgan Lee: For hosted we don't publish a single SLA number because it depends on model and region, but typical p50/p95 numbers are in our docs; for strict SLAs we recommend Dedicated. We can add a benchmark run for your traffic.
[02:58] Ruth Campbell: Security - we need SOC2, audit logs, and ability to integrate with our SSO.
[03:04] Morgan Lee: Absolutely - we support SAML SSO, RBAC, and we provide audit logs. I'll share the security pack after the call. We also have options for data retention and optional private deployments if data residency is required.
[03:18] Derek Huang: For our scoring use-case, throughput will be about 500 req/s peak with short responses. Cost is a big factor too.
[03:25] Samir Patel: For that workload we recommend batching and caching where possible - prefix caching for repeated prompts and automatic batching during low-latency windows. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization and batching configs to reduce token cost.
[03:39] [04:00] (demo continues) Samir Patel: Here's sample code - POST /v1/chat with messages, model: "redwood-small-gpt-8k" (example). Params: temperature=0.1, top_p=0.9, max_tokens=64, stream=true.
[04:20] Samir Patel: Notice the response chunks include event types: data, done, error. If you see a network error mid-stream you can replay with same idempotency token to get the canonical result.
[04:34] Ruth Campbell: Are there per-route quotas? We have different teams so we'd need rate limiting per API key.
[04:40] Morgan Lee: Yes we support per-key quotas and per-route usage reporting in the Console - token-level metrics, per-model breakdown, and trace hooks so you can see request/response times.
[04:55] Lena Ortiz: How do you handle large context windows and KV cache? We have long conversation history.
[05:01] Samir Patel: We do KV caching for keys that can be reused; for very long context we recommend chunking or retrieval-augmented generation. Kernel selection and quantization affects memory; our runtime picks optimal kernels based on seq length. (note: some words transcribed as kernal/kernal selection)
[05:18] [06:00] Ruth Campbell: On retries, do you have guidance for idempotency token generation?
[06:06] Samir Patel: Use a UUID per logical request (e.g., userID+requestHash). Also consider dedup window - we keep tokens for a short TTL. We'll send the spec.
[06:15] Derek Huang: For cost - how do we estimate tokenization differences? Some of our prompts are structured and long.
[06:21] Iris Chen: We provide token calculators in Console and sample scripts to measure tokens per prompt. Also we can run sample batches against your prompts to estimate per-1000-token cost.
[06:34] Morgan Lee: Quick interruption - are there any regulatory/data residency requirements?
[06:38] Ruth Campbell: Not yet, but we may need EU residency for some customers.
[06:42] Morgan Lee: We have region-aware routing and private deployment options. For EU residency we can route to EU hosted infra or discuss Private.
[06:51] [10:00] (mid-demo Q&A, demo paused)
[10:05] Mark Avery: Can you elaborate on audit logs? We need row-level logging for access patterns.
[10:09] Samir Patel: Our audit logs capture API key usage, request metadata, and you can export to S3 or SIEM. Full request/response logging is optional and can be toggled for compliance - by default we store metadata and traces.
[10:26] Ruth Campbell: If we try a trial, how fast can we get keys and ramp to 500rps?
[10:31] Morgan Lee: We can issue trial keys today; to ramp to steady 500rps we'd coordinate with infra and maybe use a staging Dedicated pool for predictable throughput if you need strict latency. For hosted we can support bursts but Dedicated gives reserved capacity.
[10:50] Derek Huang: Any known performance diffs vs other vendors?
[10:54] Iris Chen: Performance depends on model and quantization; our focus is to keep costs predictable. We showed numbers in our benchmark doc comparing p95 latency on comparable GPUs, but we can run the same harness on your traffic.
[11:10] Ruth Campbell: Let's talk about retries again - what do you recommend for streaming clients in case of network flakiness?
[11:15] Samir Patel: Client should buffer received tokens and use the idempotency token when replaying. If your client got partial stream, replay to retrieve canonical full stream. For some critical flows we recommend server-side checkpoints and sequence numbers.
[11:32] Lena Ortiz: Are SDKs available? We prefer official SDKs over hand-rolling.
[11:36] Morgan Lee: Yes, official SDKs for Python, Node, and a lightweight Go client. They include streaming helpers and retry middleware.
[11:46] [20:00] (deep dive on sample integration)
[20:05] Samir Patel: Walkthrough of sample python script - shows streaming handler, token buffer, and sample metric emission to Prometheus. Note transcription sometimes writes promethus without the o.
[20:27] Derek Huang: Do you offer model version pinning? We need stable outputs for offline evaluation.
[20:31] Morgan Lee: Yes, you can pin model versions and rollouts; Console supports canary rollouts and A/B tests with automatic fallback policies.
[20:42] Ruth Campbell: About pricing - are there tiers for hosted versus dedicated?
[20:46] Morgan Lee: Hosted is usage-based; Dedicated is reserved capacity with commit. We'll share the pricing sheet.
[20:55] [30:00] (closing Q&A and recap)
[30:10] Morgan Lee: Recap - we'll share pricing and trial keys, Samir will share benchmark guide and sample scripts, Ruth will send sample traffic profile and Mark will request security checklist. Any other questions?
[30:25] Ruth Campbell: No, that's great. Can we schedule the latency POC for next Wed?
[30:30] Morgan Lee: Yes - I'll follow up with a calendar invite.
[30:35] Derek Huang: One last question - what about function/tool calling and structured outputs?
[30:40] Iris Chen: We support structured output spec and function calling primitives similar to open patterns; you can define JSON schemas and the model will attempt to conform, with validation hooks.
[30:55] Mark Avery: Please include SOC2 and KMS/HSM info in the security pack.
[31:00] Morgan Lee: Will do.
[31:05] (wrap)
[31:10] Morgan Lee: Thanks everyone, we'll send the follow-ups.
[31:15] Ruth Campbell: Thanks, bye.

Post-call notes: Minor ASR artifacts: Redwood sometimes transcribed as 'Red wood', 'kernal selection' appeared as 'kernal', 'promethus' for Prometheus. Action items captured separately.
